title: A quantitative phase-field model for grain boundary trapping and diffusion of hydrogen
authors: Vincent Feyen, Martin Diehl, Nele Moelans
abstract: Grain boundaries influence hydrogen transport in polycrystalline metals by acting as both trapping sites and interconnected diffusion pathways. Conventional interpretations of thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) and permeation experiments often treat traps as isolated defects, neglecting grain boundary connectivity and potentially misinterpreting experimental data. Here, we develop a quantitative phase-field model for hydrogen diffusion, grain boundary trapping, and grain boundary-assisted transport. The formulation preserves the physical grain boundary volume independently of the numerical interface thickness and accounts for anisotropic diffusion parallel and perpendicular to grain boundaries. Benchmark simulations verify quantitative behavior under interface upscaling. The model shows that grain boundary diffusion can significantly shift TDS peaks, making Kissinger-type analyses unreliable when grain boundary transport is significant. Effective diffusion coefficients are also shown to depend strongly on grain size, trapping free energy, temperature, and grain boundary mobility. These results highlight the coupled role of trapping thermodynamics, bulk diffusion, and grain-boundary transport.
summary: This work introduces a quantitative phase-field model to accurately simulate hydrogen diffusion and trapping in polycrystalline metals, explicitly accounting for the interconnected nature of grain boundaries. It corrects deficiencies in older models by treating GBs as continuous pathways rather than isolated traps. The results show that grain boundary transport fundamentally alters measurable properties like TDS spectra and effective diffusion coefficients.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitations of conventional hydrogen trapping models that fail to account for the interconnected nature of grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline metals.
main_result: The quantitative phase-field model demonstrates that grain boundary diffusion significantly shifts TDS peaks, invalidating simple Kissinger-type analyses, and shows effective diffusion coefficients depend strongly on multiple material parameters.
method: A quantitative phase-field model is developed to simulate coupled hydrogen diffusion, trapping, and transport along grain boundaries.
model_or_system: The system is hydrogen diffusing and trapping in polycrystalline metals with a static microstructure. The model uses phase-field methods to describe the microstructure and solves coupled differential equations for hydrogen site fractions in both the bulk lattice and the GB regions.
key_observables: Total trapped hydrogen content, hydrogen fluxes (parallel/perpendicular to GBs), effective diffusion coefficients ($D_{eff,ss}$), and TDS peak shifts.
important_parameters: Grain size, trapping free energy ($\Delta\mu_{H,b,GB}$), temperature, and grain boundary mobility.
main_assumptions: The microstructure is assumed static (no grain movement), and the model neglects mechanical effects like stress-assisted diffusion.
figures_summary: Figure 12 shows the relative error in total hydrogen concentration over time for a perpendicular flux benchmark. Figure 13 compares simulated effective steady-state diffusion coefficients against an analytical fit.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the quantitative phase-field model framework, then applies it to benchmark simulations (e.g., perpendicular flux) to validate the methodology, and finally applies it to interpret experimental observables like TDS spectra and effective diffusion coefficients.
why_interesting: While focused on materials science, the rigorous development of a coupled, multi-scale transport model involving equilibrium constraints and anisotropic diffusion echoes complex non-equilibrium dynamics found in open quantum systems or reaction-diffusion processes.
